story_text.value:
I'm 17, and I started NotBot a few months ago to see whether I could turn an idea into a working project. My main interest is economics, not becoming a programmer, but I enjoy experimenting with code.

A few months ago, I had the idea of creating a program that would analyze the most recent news about a specific stock and calculate a weighted average of their polarity to create a sort of sentiment indicator.

While researching, I found a YouTube video about creating a simple GitHub repository that did, in a simplified and imprecise way, what I had in mind. At first glance, I realized it was a very simple program: feedparser retrieved news from Google News, beautifulsoup4 extracted the content, the sentiment was analyzed with FinBERT, running through Transformers and PyTorch.

From there, I started modifying it with the free versions of Gemini. I had to solve a lot of problems, for example fixing the extraction of articles from Google News, I managed to solve it with a new library (googlenewsdecoder).

Then I had to replace FinBERT, because it classified sentiment based on the context of the words but didn't take into account the actual impact of the event using external sources.

I experimented with an LLM that allowed me to specify the evaluation criteria more precisely through a prompt. I found a free one with rather strict TPM and RPM limits (it was called openai/gpt-oss-120b).

I also created two coefficients: one that adjusted the reliability of the news based on its source, and another that adjusted its impact based on how recent it was (all selected news articles had been published within the last 24 hours). Each article was divided into title, description, and content, and each of these three sections had a different weight based on predefined values (title 35%, description 25%, and text 40%). If the content had fewer than 100 characters, the text was not assigned any weight, and the title accounted for 60% while the description accounted for 40%.

After these modifications, I took a break of about a month because of school commitments, during which I discovered Codex (OpenAI's agent).

I changed the main LLM and implemented Gemini (3.1 Flash-Lite) because the TPM limits of the LLM I was using were too restrictive.

Even though I started using Gemini, I didn't discard Groq. In fact, I used it as a fallback in case Gemini returned some kind of error.

Another important modification was the addition of asynchronous article downloading through aiohttp and the processing of multiple articles simultaneously through asyncio. Later, I decided to start using Groq again for article analysis. In fact, I had both LLMs analyze the longer articles and then calculated the average of their two polarity scores.

The first was Finnhub, which allowed me to search for many more news articles about a specific stock (by entering its name and ticker).

At that point, I had to split up the code because the script had become very long.

The last modification I made concerned news selection: I implemented a filter that prevented similar news articles from being selected, to avoid excessively distorting the polarity in an incorrect way.

First of all, I'd like to know, from an expert, how well the project is built from a structural point of view and how it could be improved. For future projects, what parameters should I take into consideration to understand whether a project is well built?

Secondly, I'd like to know how I can determine whether a program like this can actually work, or at least how it could be useful (even with some modifications).

The third and final point is: which aspects of the pipeline might require more attention or could be optimized? Does it make sense to continue working on the project (also with the idea of turning it into a product), or am I approaching a structural limit?

title.value: Show HN: My first project, an AI-powered financial news analyzer

story_text.value:
Hi, this is a package I developed for keeping track of short toy-model development cycles and explaining what changed between runs.

The core idea: commands run through the package, and their declared parameters (or injected parameters with --substitute) and outcomes go into a dependency-free ledger stored in the project. Because that ledger lives in the project directory, it has worked well for passing context between different agents. I’ve also found some use for it in CI work.

title.value: Show HN: Record, branch, and compare command runs in stdlib-only Python

story_text.value:
I own a reMarkable 2 and wanted more to read on it than my own PDFs, so I built a free web app. You connect your tablet once with the official one-time code, then:

- Send any of 79,000+ public-domain books (Standard Ebooks first, plus Project Gutenberg, Wikisource and OpenStax textbooks).

- Get comics (xkcd volumes with the hover text, Pepper&Carrot, pre-1931 strips) and 33,000+ magazine issues from 1930 and earlier, re-rendered for e-ink.

- Get puzzle books (sudoku with unique solutions, mazes, nonograms) to solve with the pen.

- Subscribe to 160+ blogs and news sites; it builds one EPUB edition every morning or every six hours, and moves editions you've finished to the trash.

Each kind lands in its own folder, so notebooks are never touched. Built with Node and the reMarkable cloud API. No ads, no tracking, free. Feedback very welcome.

title.value: Show HN: Fireside Folio – free books, comics and news editions for reMarkable

story_text.value:
I built a 4-channel music tracker modeled on the original Game Boy's sound hardware: two pulse channels, a wave channel, and noise. It runs entirely in the browser using the Web Audio API, with no account or backend.

Songs save to localStorage, and share links compress the whole song into the URL hash, so sharing never touches a server. You can also export WAV, M4A, or a square MP4 of the rows playing.

It ships with 3 demo songs to show what it can do. I’m a developer, not a composer, so I made the song format LLM-friendly: use “Import from text” on the home page, and see https://chiptunes.studio/llms.txt for the format.

To hear it first, here's a demo song. It opens on a playback page with a Remix button that drops you into the editor: https://chiptunes.studio/share#v1.7Z3BjqJAEIbfpfZKJ40gCjcV9L...

I’d love feedback from anyone with tracker or DAW experience, and I’d love to hear what you make. Share your song links!

title.value: Show HN: A free Gameboy–style music tracker in the browser with shareable URLs

story_text.value:
There is some recent discourse about what a "better" interface for humans managing agents looks like. Email/inboxes have come up, and it's reinforcing the premise of thing i've been building. e.g.

  - https://x.com/brian_armstrong/status/2119112609223827547
  - https://x.com/rough__sea/status/2119288646671155217?a=KRzp4CnuV6SijzvCTUw&s=20
This isn't 'another ADE', this is a side-car type of experience and it integrates nearly a year of work around annotating markdown, html, other artifacts since I requested the original Claude Code Hooks feature for better human-control integration.

The email inbox model is intuitive, but so could be "forums", slack-like, or other surfaces feel right.

I do not believe we will be working in coding sessions (full transcripts) much longer. I've been hitting flow-state on top of a better surface layer to make decisions and annotate artifacts, view variations, review code, etc all feedback going back to the agents

MIT/Apache2.0:

https://github.com/backnotprop/plannotator

title.value: Show HN: Email-like interface to review, decide, and annotate agent work

story_text.value:
I've made AntiFind, to allow you to search everywhere at once, vastly increasing the efficiency of LLMs and your own searches:

AntiFind indexes filesystems, not folders.

It maintains a live view of storage by reading filesystem metadata directly. Because it understands the underlying filesystems, it can search across storage that the operating system is not currently exposing, including unmounted partitions.

Allowing you to search for and play media from Linux in your Windows and the other way around. Without mounting the drives.

This works on Linux, Windows and MacOS.

The underlying idea is simple: instead of walking directories, read the filesystem's file tables directly.

Most tools discover the filesystem again every time you search. AntiFind reads the drive's metadata in one pass and then follows changes as they happen.

AntiFind supports Windows, Linux and macOS. It includes both a GUI and a command line. The CLI supports JSON output (--json) and was designed to integrate cleanly with automation and LLM workflows.

There's a lot more to it, and you can find timings on my site, but that's the core idea.

More information: https://antisoftworks.com/antifind

Cheers!

title.value: Show HN: Search Everywhere at Once. Instantly
